blocks.text: Global business development means building business activity across national borders. A firm may seek new customers, spread fixed costs over a larger output, access resources or reduce dependence on one domestic market. Expansion can also minimise losses when demand falls at home, although entering a new market introduces costs and uncertainty.

A larger potential market is an opportunity, rather than evidence that expansion will be profitable. Compare expected additional revenue with production, adaptation, transport, finance and compliance costs. Consider whether the business has the capacity and working capital to deliver.

Consumer purchasing patterns describe what, when, where and how people buy. Spending patterns show how consumers allocate expenditure across products and services. Income, household structure, culture, digital access and preferences can make an overseas segment different from the domestic market.

For an Australian food producer, a market with growing demand for convenient packaged meals may offer an opportunity. The firm still needs evidence about acceptable prices, serving sizes, local competition and distribution. National averages can conceal large differences between consumer groups.

The World Trade Organization provides a framework of agreed trade rules, negotiations and dispute settlement between members. Predictable rules can reduce uncertainty for exporters. Tariffs, licensing and other barriers still affect the cost and feasibility of trade.

Distinguish trade countermeasures authorised through WTO processes from sanctions imposed by governments under other frameworks. A business must check the actual restrictions applying to the product, customer and destination. Membership of an international organisation does not mean unrestricted access to every market.

Deregulation removes or relaxes particular restrictions on financial activity, potentially increasing competition, access to capital and cross-border investment. A business might obtain finance from a wider range of institutions or investors, helping it fund expansion.

Greater access can also expose firms to exchange-rate changes, volatile capital flows and unsuitable financial products. Deregulation does not mean the absence of prudential, consumer protection or financial crime rules. Evaluate how a specific change affects financing cost, availability and risk.

Illustrative case: an Australian outdoor equipment business faces a small domestic market and sees demand overseas. Online purchasing makes customers easier to reach, while trade arrangements may reduce eligible import tariffs. The firm considers additional capacity and foreign-currency receipts.

A strong response connects each driver to a business consequence: demand could raise revenue, spreading fixed costs may reduce average cost, and foreign-currency exposure could make returns less predictable. Recommend a pilot market when demand evidence and delivery capacity remain uncertain.

Globalisation increases connections between national economies through trade, investment, labour, knowledge and technology. Businesses can source inputs, coordinate production and serve customers across borders. Domestic businesses also face stronger competition from overseas suppliers.

Benefits and costs are distributed unevenly. Lower prices and greater choice may benefit consumers, while an import-competing producer may lose sales. Analyse the affected stakeholder, the mechanism and the time period instead of describing globalisation as universally beneficial or harmful.

Offshore production can create jobs and training opportunities in host countries while reducing demand for some roles in the home country. Other home-country jobs may grow in design, logistics or management. Effects depend on skills, investment, labour standards and the industry.

International teams, licensing and supplier relationships can spread skills and production techniques. Benefits require training, infrastructure and the ability to use new technology. A firm should consider retraining and transition support where its restructuring displaces workers.

International cooperation can simplify standards, improve infrastructure and help firms resolve cross-border problems. Larger markets can support specialisation and economies of scale. At the same time, domestic firms may need better quality, innovation or service to compete with global brands.

A local manufacturer might concentrate on custom designs and reliable support rather than matching the lowest import price. Explain how differentiation creates value for a specific customer group, and whether customers are willing to pay enough to cover the additional cost.

A tax haven generally offers very low taxation and may offer limited transparency. Multinational firms can have incentives to locate activities or profits in lower-tax jurisdictions. Tax minimisation, unlawful evasion and aggressive avoidance are different concepts; a low tax bill alone does not establish illegality.

Transfer pricing concerns prices used in transactions between related entities, such as a parent company and an overseas subsidiary. These transactions are legitimate, but artificial pricing can shift reported profits. Applicable tax rules generally require related-party transactions to reflect arm’s-length conditions. Businesses must consider compliance, reputation and their contribution to public services.

Home-grown or locally developed products may support local employment, regional expertise and shorter supply chains. Familiarity with local preferences, traceability and an authentic origin story can strengthen differentiation and customer trust. Local development can also build skills and intellectual property.

These advantages are conditional. Local production does not automatically mean lower environmental impact or better quality, and origin claims must be accurate. Evaluate price, performance and credible evidence alongside community benefits. A business needs a proposition customers value, rather than relying on origin alone.

Ethical decision-making considers effects on workers, customers, communities and the environment alongside commercial objectives. A decision may satisfy a local legal minimum yet raise concerns about fairness or environmental harm. A global business needs clear standards and a process for identifying and addressing risks.

Consider the proposed activity, affected stakeholders, likely consequences and practical alternatives. Explain both immediate costs and longer-term effects such as trust, supplier reliability and reputation. Ethical practice requires evidence and follow-through.

Outsourcing contracts an activity to another organisation; offshoring moves an activity to another country. They can occur together or separately. Reasons include specialist skills, capacity, market access and lower operating costs.

Risks include poor working conditions, reduced oversight, quality problems and disruption. Due diligence should examine suppliers and subcontractors, worker safety, hours, pay and grievance channels. A supplier code without monitoring or corrective action offers limited protection. Responsible purchasing prices and lead times also matter.

International expansion can increase transport, energy use, water demand and waste. Businesses can assess lifecycle effects, improve resource efficiency, select lower-impact materials and work with suppliers on emissions and waste reduction.

A cheaper supplier may impose environmental costs on its community. Compare alternatives using credible data and disclose the scope and limitations of claims. A recyclable package alone does not establish that the entire product is environmentally sustainable.

A home government may support exporters through eligible grants, advice or tax measures. A host government may offer investment grants, tax concessions or infrastructure to attract business activity and employment. Such incentives can reduce entry costs or improve expected returns.

Eligibility, funding limits, reporting conditions and repayment provisions can apply. A grant is not guaranteed revenue until relevant conditions are satisfied. Assess whether the investment remains viable after an incentive expires, and distinguish an incentive from a permanent competitive advantage.

Illustrative case: a manufacturer can obtain a host-country tax concession and lower production costs, but an audit identifies unsafe supplier practices. A sound recommendation compares the commercial opportunity with remediation costs and responsibilities to workers.

The business could require corrective action, support training and phase orders while monitoring improvements. If serious risks cannot be controlled, it may need an alternative supplier. Explain how the proposal protects people and the business, rather than treating a concession as sufficient justification.

A free trade agreement is a treaty through which participating economies agree to reduce specified barriers and establish rules for trade, services and investment. It may lower eligible tariffs, improve customs processes and make market access more predictable.

An FTA does not remove every business cost or regulatory requirement. Product standards, biosecurity, taxes, licensing and rules of origin may still apply. Compare the agreement’s actual treatment of the product and destination rather than assuming every imported good becomes cheaper.

The ASEAN–Australia–New Zealand Free Trade Area connects Australia, New Zealand and participating ASEAN economies through trade and investment commitments. Its framework includes goods, services, investment and cooperation. Tariff treatment depends on the relevant schedules and product rules.

Rules of origin establish whether a product qualifies for preferential treatment. Customs evidence and certification requirements matter. A business may need to compare overlapping agreements, because a different agreement may offer a more suitable tariff or origin rule for the same shipment.

bme-y12-u3-free-trade-agreements.title: How an exporter uses an agreement

blocks.text: An exporter identifies the product classification, checks the destination’s tariff schedule and tests the relevant rule of origin. It then arranges the required origin evidence and customs documents. Accurate information reduces delay and the risk of a rejected preference claim.

Illustrative example: a food producer using imported ingredients cannot assume that packaging in Australia makes its goods eligible. It must check the product-specific origin test. Freight, distributor margins and compliance costs still affect the final customer price after a tariff reduction.

The Australia New Zealand Closer Economic Relations Trade Agreement supports close economic integration between Australia and New Zealand. It provides duty-free treatment for goods meeting its origin requirements and supports trade in services and cooperation.

CER operates alongside related arrangements that reduce trans-Tasman barriers. Businesses must still check requirements such as biosecurity, product compliance and any exceptions. Shared standards in some areas do not mean every regulation is identical or that every government assistance program is prohibited.

Some domestic firms lose market share

blocks.text: Trade can improve resource allocation and access to inputs and technology. Adjustment can also involve job losses, competitive pressure and environmental concerns. These outcomes are not automatic and do not affect every industry equally.

For an Australian exporter, weigh additional demand and tariff savings against adaptation, logistics and documentation costs. Identify a specific advantage, explain how it changes the firm’s position and consider the strongest limitation.

An FTA can make entry more attractive without making it viable. A trial through a local distributor might provide evidence about demand before the exporter commits to a large overseas operation. Use current official agreement guidance for actual commercial decisions.

E-commerce uses digital networks to conduct commercial transactions. A business can sell through its own website, a marketplace or a business-to-business portal. Digital channels can make overseas discovery, ordering and payment easier without initially establishing a physical retail network.

Potential reach does not equal effective demand. Language, local payment preferences, internet access, trust and delivery costs affect conversion. A marketplace can provide customer access while charging fees and limiting control over the customer relationship.

Plan discovery, product information, checkout, payment, fulfilment, support and returns as one system. Show accurate prices, currency, delivery times and relevant charges. Localised information can reduce abandoned orders and complaints.

A customer may accept a product price but reject the order once freight and import charges appear. Clear landed-cost information and practical returns arrangements can therefore be more valuable than simply attracting more visitors.

Cross-border selling requires inventory accuracy, reliable shipping, appropriate customs documents and support across time zones. Cybersecurity, privacy, fraud and payment disputes need active controls. Consumer and tax obligations may differ across markets.

Evaluate platform reliability and supplier dependencies. A sudden increase in orders can damage a brand if stock or delivery capacity is insufficient. Start with achievable service promises, monitor fulfilment and expand when the operation can consistently meet them.

Track visits, conversion rate, average order value, delivery performance, returns and contribution after channel and freight costs. Segment results by market rather than relying on a combined sales total.

Illustrative example: 2,000 relevant visits generate 60 orders, a 3% conversion rate. If each order contributes $12 after variable costs, the orders contribute $720 before campaign and fixed costs. Compare this with acquisition spending before describing the trial as successful.
